results.title: Importing Auto Parts into US: 2026 Section 232 Guide
results.content:
The rules for importing auto parts into the US changed dramatically in May 2025, when a 25 percent Section 232 tariff hit engines, transmissions, powertrain components, and electrical parts — regardless of country of origin. Add the standard 2.5 percent base duty, USMCA content carve-outs, EPA and DOT compliance, and the reality that a single misclassified shipment can wipe out a quarter's margin, and you have one of the most complex commercial import categories in the country today. This [...] Most auto parts imported into the US in 2026 face a 25 percent Section 232 tariff that took effect May 3, 2025. The tariff applies to engines, engine parts, transmissions, powertrain components, and electrical components for passenger vehicles and light trucks, regardless of country of origin. USMCA-qualifying parts from Canada and Mexico are exempt or partially exempt during a transition period. The base Harmonized Tariff Schedule duty on most auto parts is around 2.5 percent, but the Section [...] ### What Section 232 covers for auto parts

The 25 percent tariff applies to auto parts for passenger vehicles and light trucks, specifically including:

 Engines and engine parts
 Transmissions
 Powertrain components (driveshafts, axles, differentials)
 Electrical components
 Additional parts may be added through subsequent rulemaking

results.title: Auto Tariffs 101: How U.S. Car Import Duties Really Work in 2025
results.content:
Brake pads (China): $100 → $125
 German transmission: $3,000 → $3,750
 Electronics module: $500 → $625

Even parts that were previously low-cost or sourced globally are now scrutinized for tariff exposure.

### 🏭 For “American-Made” Cars

No car is 100% U.S.-made. Many U.S.-assembled vehicles still rely on foreign components that are now subject to import tariffs: [...] Engines, transmissions, electronic control units (ECUs), brakes, steering systems, and hundreds more
 Each imported part is taxed individually unless exempted (e.g., USMCA-compliant)
 As of May 3, 2025, a 25% rate applies to non-exempt parts

### 🔩 Materials (Steel, Aluminum)

 Tariffs on raw materials are handled separately — often 25–50%
 Automotive-specific tariffs usually override metal tariffs to prevent double taxation (“destacking” rules) [...] In short, nearly every component in the automotive supply chain — from engines to electrical modules — can now face import duties depending on where it’s made and whether it qualifies for trade agreement exemptions.

## Auto Tariffs by Country: No Longer One Rate for All
